Experiment 1 (array size 2/6/8/12): a walkthrough of the results

Regression to the mean in perceptual experience — exploratory, not the main write-up

19 September 2026

About this document

Experiment 1 - array size (2/6/8/12). Arrays of 2, 6, 8 or 12 coloured squares (24 trials per array size, 96 per session). Noise was manipulated through the number of squares; each array size always used the same fixed offsets around the mean. Participants reported the colour on a 50-step scale, either the average colour or how red/blue the array felt (experience condition).

This document walks through every result of this experiment: first whether the data and the manipulation are sound, then what they show about regression to the mean (RttM) in perceptual experience. Every number and figure is recomputed from the analysis pipeline when the file is knitted; it is exploratory and not part of the main write-up. True values are the mean of the squares actually shown (EPOC_TRUE_VALUE = "shown").

Two directions of RttM. Forward: given a stimulus, is the report less extreme? (slope of report on true value). Reverse: given a report, was the stimulus less extreme? (the exaggeration claim: extreme experiences overstate the world). Pure noise produces reverse RttM but leaves the forward slope at 1, so a forward slope below 1 needs more than noise.

Bottom line

Regression to the mean, but no reliable effect of array size on it. Reports tracked the stimulus less tightly at some array sizes (correlation .80 / .76 / .72 / .76, p = .001), but not in design order: tracking was worst at 8 squares, and 8- and 12-square arrays are equally dispersed. The forward slope (.89 / .82 / .76 / .81) changes in the participant-level test (p = .013) but not in the strict mixed model (p = .15), and reports do not narrow reliably (p = .27). Extreme reports come from less extreme stimuli at every array size (reverse slope about .6). At the extremes, the differences between 2 and 12 squares point in opposite directions at the two ends (+1.3 units for high reports, −1.7 for low reports, as given): that is the overall shift of 2-square reports (about 2.4 units low), not a change in exaggeration, and nothing remains once each participant’s shift is removed.

Key results at a glance (levels in design order; array size is not the order of colour dispersion, see section 2)

Participant flow

  • Trials analysed: average 2,111 (about 92 per participant, mean absolute error 5.05 units); experience 1,923 (about 92 per participant, mean absolute error 4.99 units).
  • Cleaning, identical for all experiments: second sessions dropped; reports of 0 treated as missing (the response scale’s starting value, saved when someone clicks without crossing the scale); RT < 200 ms or > 8 s; ±2.5 SD RT trimming per participant; errors ≥ 30 units; participants keeping < 85% of trials or with Spearman r ≤ .30.

2. Does the manipulation work?

Stimulus checks (true value = mean of the squares shown)
Level Spread within arrays (SD) Spread of true means (SD) Mean true value
2 squares 4.00 6.60 25.29
6 squares 4.32 6.69 25.37
8 squares 5.48 6.62 25.19
12 squares 5.45 6.64 25.55

The spread of true means across trials is the same at every level, so only the arrays themselves differ between levels. Each level always used the same template of offsets, so the array make-up does not vary within a level and cannot be tested against the report.

Problems found.

  1. Array size does not track colour dispersion. The fixed templates give within-array spreads of about 4.0 / 4.3 / 5.5 / 5.5, so 8- and 12-square arrays are equally dispersed. Array size is therefore not a clean noise manipulation.
  2. The 12-square template does not average to zero (the squares shown average 0.33 above the logged mean). This document uses the mean of the squares actually shown as the true value, which removes the problem.
  3. 2-square arrays read low (about 2.4 units below the mean shown). This is not explained by the colour scale, and only slightly (if at all) by weighting the lighter square; nearly identical practice pairs read low too.
  4. Trial order: 2-square trials come slightly earlier in each colour block (the same biased-shuffle signature as Experiment 4; the Experiment 1 task code actually run has not been checked).
  5. One-step colour offset between stimulus squares and response images (same images as Experiment 4): a perfect observer would report about 1 unit low; this does not affect slopes or comparisons between levels.

5. Why the forward slope changes: noise and narrowing

Slope = correlation × (SD of reports / SD of true values); values centred within participant
Level Within-array SD r SD true SD reports SD ratio Slope Calibrated slope (r²) Reverse slope
2 squares 4.00 0.744 6.56 7.81 1.19 0.89 0.55 0.63
6 squares 4.32 0.703 6.64 7.75 1.17 0.82 0.49 0.60
8 squares 5.48 0.665 6.58 7.48 1.14 0.75 0.44 0.59
12 squares 5.45 0.700 6.61 7.69 1.16 0.82 0.49 0.60

From 2 squares to 12 squares: log change in slope -0.084, of which 73% from the correlation and 27% from the SD ratio (within participants: correlation p = .034, ratio p = .274). Pure noise would raise the ratio as the correlation falls; a falling ratio is a genuine narrowing of the reports. A calibrated observer’s forward slope would equal r²; slopes above that mean people correct less than their noise warrants, which leaves extreme reports exaggerated (reverse slope = r² / forward slope).

How much more the same extreme report exaggerated its stimulus at 12 squares than at 2 squares (positive = more exaggeration at the higher level)
Extreme reports Participant-level + trial position + position, reweighted
High (≥ 36) as given +1.33, p = .007 +1.39, p = .005 +1.29, p = .011
Low (≤ 14) as given -1.67, p = .009 -1.65, p = .009 -1.54, p = .015

Low (≤ 14) shift removed -0.35, p = .569 -0.26, p = .663 -0.17, p = .782

Only trials with the same report value are compared. “Shift removed” subtracts each participant’s average reporting error at each level first, so a general tendency to answer high or low at one level cannot look like exaggeration at one end; it removes only a constant, not the regression itself. “Reweighted” gives every level the same distribution of true values.
